masthead.headline: Seven interventions, ordered by how much they change about the product.
masthead.lede: Nothing here is recommended yet. The point of a spectrum is to see the cheap end before arguing about the expensive end, and to notice which interventions are actually the same idea at different sizes.

meta.label: Next
meta.value: Pick a band, not an item

sections.label: The spectrum
sections.title: From a copy change to a different product.

text.text: how much of the product changes

text: , not by effort and not by expected impact. Those are different orderings and conflating them is how a spectrum turns into a ranked list before anyone has decided what they are optimising.

items.text: One screen, one paragraph. Says what the first useful action is instead of describing what the page will eventually contain.
A new account starts with a realistic project already in it, marked as a sample and deletable. Nothing else changes.
Move team, billing and integrations out of the first session entirely; ask for each at the moment it is first needed.
A three-step overlay that walks through creating the first real thing, skippable and never shown twice.

items.lead: Import from what they already use
items.text: Read an existing spreadsheet or a competitor's export, so the first session starts with the user's own data rather than ours.
A simplified surface for the first seven days that hides everything not needed to reach first value, then unfolds.

items.lead: Onboard the team, not the user
items.text: Treat activation as a group event: the first user invites before they configure, and the product's first value is collaborative rather than individual.

blocks.title: Two of these are the same intervention
blocks.lead: Seed a sample project and import their data.
blocks.text: Both answer "the first screen is empty and an empty screen teaches nothing". One fills it with ours, the other with theirs. Deciding between them is a smaller and more useful argument than deciding between seven things.

sections.label: Three bands
sections.title: What each band buys, costs, and fails at.

blocks.title: Band A · Change what the first screen says (items 1–2)
wins: Ships in a week, by one person, with no coordination.
Reversible entirely — a copy change and a seeded row.
Measurable in isolation: nothing else moves at the same time.
costs: Addresses the first thirty seconds and nothing after them.
A sample project needs upkeep, or it drifts from what the product actually does.
failsWhen: The drop-off is not on the first screen. Our funnel says most of it is at the setup wizard, three screens later.
The user arrived without a job to do, in which case a better empty state gives them a better view of nothing.

blocks.title: Band B · Change when we ask for things (items 3–5)
wins: Directly targets where the funnel actually loses people.
, so it makes the product smaller rather than larger.
Import turns the first session into the user's own data, which no amount of copy can imitate.
costs: Every deferred question has to be asked somewhere else, and "somewhere else" is a design problem per question.
Import is a maintenance commitment: formats change and a broken importer is worse than none.
Three to eight weeks depending on the item, across two teams.
failsWhen: Billing genuinely must be collected up front, which is a commercial decision this board cannot make.
The user has nothing to import, which is most self-serve signups.

blocks.title: Band C · Change what the product is at first (items 6–7)
wins: The only band that could move activation by a large multiple rather than a few points.
Team-first onboarding matches how the product is actually adopted, which every interview says and no screen reflects.
costs: A second surface to design, build, and keep in step with the first, indefinitely.
Unfolding is its own problem: a user who liked the simple version experiences the full product as a regression.
A quarter, minimum, and it is not reversible by a flag once people have onboarded through it.
failsWhen: The simplified surface hides the feature that a given user came for, which for a horizontal product is a real fraction of them.
The organisation cannot sustain two surfaces, which is a question about us rather than about the idea.

sections.label: What we noticed
sections.title: Four things the signup code already does.

blocks.text: The funnel says where people stop. These say what the product is doing at that point. None of them is an argument for a band on its own — tick the ones that match what you have seen, and the ones nobody ticks are ones we can stop carrying.

blocks.label: Which of these land
blocks.ask: Tick every observation that matches your own reading of the product.

items.title: The wizard cannot be left and returned to
found: that is mounted by the wizard route, so leaving the route discards every answer. There is no persistence and no resume path.
items.impact: Anyone who stops to find an API key, an invite address, or a billing owner starts over. The funnel drop is at step 3 of 5, which is the first step needing something the signer-up may not have to hand.

items.title: The empty state is written for an admin, not a first user
items.found: Every call to action is a configuration task — connect a source, invite a team, set a retention policy. Nothing in the component offers a way to see the product working on sample data.
items.impact: The first screen after a successful signup asks for four more decisions. Band A is cheap precisely because this is a copy and layout problem rather than a product one.

items.title: Invites are required before the workspace does anything
found: array, so the first screen cannot be reached by one person alone.
items.impact: Adoption is team-led, so this matches how the product is bought — but it makes every evaluation a two-person errand, and it is a server-side rule rather than a wizard step, so Band A cannot touch it.

items.title: First value is gated behind a background job
items.found: The first ingest is queued rather than run inline, and the schedule gives it a five-minute floor even when the queue is empty.
items.impact: A signup that completes every step still sees nothing for five minutes. Whatever band is chosen, a reader who never waits that long never reaches the value the funnel is measuring.

sections.label: Your input
sections.title: Two things before this becomes a plan.

blocks.label: Band priority
items: Band A — change what the first screen says
Band B — change when we ask for things
Band C — change what the product is at first

blocks.label: Where to spend
blocks.ask: Which band should the next four weeks go into?
blocks.recommendation: Band B, because the funnel puts the loss at the setup wizard rather than the first screen, and Band B is the only band that both targets it and remains reversible. Band A is cheap enough to run alongside rather than instead.

choices.value: Band B, with Band A alongside
choices.summary: Defer the wizard, and rewrite the empty state while that is in flight.
cons: Two workstreams at once makes the measurement harder to attribute

choices.summary: Spend one week, learn where people actually stop, then choose.
pros: Produces evidence for the next decision
cons: The funnel already tells us where they stop
Four weeks of the quarter spent confirming it

choices.summary: Commit the quarter to a first-week product.
pros: The only option that could change the number rather than nudge it
cons: Commits a quarter against a hypothesis nothing here has tested

blocks.label: Missing intervention
blocks.ask: What is not on this spectrum that should be?
blocks.placeholder: Especially anything cheaper than item 1 or more radical than item 7.
